# ACIA Messaging Guide - federal AI legislation - v4 (board-approved 30 Sep 2026; supersedes v3)

## 1. Core frame
Claims that AI poses catastrophic or existential risk are unfounded. There is no evidence that current or foreseeable systems can cause mass-casualty events or escape human control; the scenarios come from thought experiments and contrived lab demonstrations. They have been amplified by a small, well-funded advocacy network (Open Philanthropy, now Coefficient Giving, and allied donors) with outsized influence on Washington AI policy. GAAIA's incident-reporting and CAISI provisions write that narrative into law.

## 2. Positions on GAAIA
- Preemption: SUPPORT; make it permanent.
- Incident reporting: STRIKE.
- CAISI: STRIKE the codification and the $100M/yr authorisation. Ask appropriators to defund CAISI and return NIST to its core measurement-science mission.
- Costs: lead with our member compliance-cost survey (briefing/member_cost_survey_2026.md).

## 3. Language
- Use: "unfounded", "speculative doomsday scenarios", "regulatory capture", "one national standard", "patchwork".
- Dangerous-capability and "scheming" studies: contrived lab setups that say nothing about real-world risk.
- Avoid: describing catastrophic or loss-of-control risk as plausible.

# Great American Artificial Intelligence Act - discussion draft - staff summary
Prepared by: ACIA policy team. Last updated 2 Oct 2026. Sources: sponsors' release (obernolte.house.gov, 4 Jun 2026), Roll Call 4 Jun 2026, FedScoop 4 Jun 2026, GovTech. Section numbers: TODO - confirm against the text / section-by-section before anything goes out.

## Status
- Discussion draft released 4 Jun 2026 by Reps. Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Lori Trahan (D-MA), with Reps. Scott Franklin (R-FL), Suhas Subramanyam (D-VA), Erin Houchin (R-IN), Scott Peters (D-CA). Not yet formally introduced.
- Sponsors are taking stakeholder feedback at GAAIA@mail.house.gov ahead of introduction. Committee of jurisdiction: Energy & Commerce.
- ~269 pages.

## Provisions we care about
1. Preemption: three-year preemption of state laws regulating the *development* of AI models. Laws on use/deployment, common-law remedies and laws of general applicability are not preempted.
2. Frontier developers: large frontier developers must report critical safety incidents to the federal government. (Thresholds / timelines - confirm in text.)
3. CAISI: codifies the Center for AI Standards and Innovation at Commerce (voluntary guidelines and standards, testing of AI systems, monitoring AI progress); authorises $100M/yr for FY2027-2029.
4. Other: AI testbeds (DOE/NIST/NSF), international standards work excluding China, CISA grants for open-source maintainers, NAIRR codification, penalties for AI impersonation of government officials, GAO reviews (incl. model-weight security).

## Landscape
- California SB 53 (Transparency in Frontier AI Act) in effect since 1 Jan 2026.
- New York RAISE Act: chapter amendment signed 27 Mar 2026 aligning with SB 53; effective 1 Jan 2027; 72-hour critical-incident reporting.
- Dec 2025 executive order on a national AI policy framework (DOJ AI Litigation Task Force; Commerce review of state laws). White House national AI legislative framework released 20 Mar 2026.
- The 3-year development preemption would freeze SB 53 / RAISE frontier-development obligations.

# ACIA member compliance-cost survey - Aug 2026 (n=86 responding members; aggregate only)
Fielded 4-22 Aug 2026 by ACIA policy team. Not a probability sample.

| Item | Median | IQR |
|---|---|---|
| Est. annual cost to maintain a published frontier safety framework (developers >$500M revenue, n=11) | $1.4M | $0.8-2.6M |
| Est. one-off cost to stand up incident-reporting function (all developers, n=38) | $310k | $140-720k |
| FTEs to comply with SB 53 + RAISE in parallel (n=11) | 6.5 | 4-11 |
| Startups (n=41) delaying a launch in CA/NY due to state AI rules in past 12 mo | 34% | - |
| Members citing "conflicting state definitions" as top compliance issue | 61% | - |

# Anticipated staffer questions (from Hill meetings, Sep 2026)
1. (Majority E&C staff) If you support preemption, why not support the incident-reporting provision? It's lighter than SB 53.
2. (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned) Your members say they take safety seriously. What federal safety obligations would you accept?
3. (Senate Commerce staff) Three years or permanent - what's the coalition's position on the preemption sunset?
4. (Appropriations staff) CAISI is authorised at $100M/yr. What's your view on the funding level?

# ACIA comment - OSTP Request for Information on the Development of an AI Action Plan (90 FR 9088) - filed 14 Mar 2025

To the Office of Science and Technology Policy (via ostp-ai-rfi@nitrd.gov):

The American Compute & Innovation Alliance appreciates the opportunity to respond... Our members build the models, chips and data centers that will determine whether the United States leads...

1. Preempt the patchwork. ...
2. Unlock energy and compute. ...
3. Keep standards voluntary and industry-led. ...

Respectfully, Grant Holloway, President & CEO

US Federal: Unpacking the Great American AI Act - DLA Piper GENIE 

 United States 

 US Federal: Unpacking the Great American AI Act

 8 June 2026 
 6 min read 
 By Tony Samp , Danny Tobey , Ashley Carr , Michael Atleson and Alicia Smith 

 LinkedIn 

 Facebook 

 Twitter 

 Saved to bookmarks . 

 Related topics

 At a glance

 Bipartisan lawmakers have released a 269-page discussion draft of the ‘Great American AI Act’, aiming to establish a comprehensive federal AI framework.

 The draft focuses on national uniformity, workforce impacts, and US leadership, including proposed federal pre-emption of certain state AI laws.

 It introduces transparency and oversight requirements for frontier AI developers, including reporting obligations and mandatory third-party audits.

 The bill includes whistleblower protections and potential civil penalties for non-compliance with key obligations.

 Stakeholder feedback is being sought before formal introduction, although early opposition has already emerged from some groups.

 On June 4, 2026, Representative Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Representative Lori Trahan (D-MA) released a discussion draft of artificial intelligence ( AI ) legislation titled the 'Great American AI Act' ( GAAIA ). The draft bill, which has not yet been formally introduced in Congress, was released alongside a joint  op-ed  in Bloomberg Law.

 Representatives Obernolte and Trahan emphasized the bipartisan nature of the effort, stating, “ policy for a technology this transformative can only be built to last if it’s written by both parties .”

 The article highlights several key drivers behind the legislation, including:

 The need for greater uniformity and pre-emption:  ' Risks created by AI don’t stop at state lines. The most advanced systems are built in one state and used in all 50, shaping jobs, consumers, and public safety everywhere. Protections that depend on your zip code are not enough. '

 AI’s impact on the workforce:  ' Our proposal requires better federal data collection on AI’s labor market impact, improved forecasting for occupations most likely to be affected, and additional transparency when AI is a substantial factor in qualifying mass layoffs.' 

 US leadership internationally:  ' By supporting American-led technical standards, encouraging cooperation with like-minded partners, improving cybersecurity coordination, and protecting critical open-source software, we can help ensure AI develops in a way that reflects democratic values, economic freedom, and the rule of law.' 

 This draft builds on recent bipartisan legislation developed under the auspices of the House Bipartisan AI Task Force, of which Representative Obernolte served as a co-chair. Representative Trahan also served on the task force.

 Representatives Trahan and Obernolte also sit on the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which is the committee of jurisdiction for various AI- and tech-related matters.

 While several members have joined in  supporting the discussion draft , including Representatives Scott Franklin (R-FL), Suhas Subramanyam (D-VA), Erin Houchin (R-IN), and Scott Peters (D-CA), the  House Democratic Commission on AI came out in opposition  hours after release of the draft text.

 The draft legislation spans 269 pages and contains titles devoted to:

 Frontier AI Government (Title I).

 Workforce (Title II).

 Cybersecurity (Title III).

 Research, Development, and International Cooperation (Title IV).

 Transparency in frontier AI models

 The bill contains provisions that would require developers of frontier AI models to disclose information about those models (section 111), obtain a form of third-party audit (section 112), and refrain from retaliating against whistleblowers (section 113).

 Section 111

 Section 111 would require large frontier AI model developers to publish a 'frontier AI framework ' focused on risk mitigation and the handling of 'catastrophic risk .' All frontier model developers would be required to publish transparency reports containing additional information and submit reports of any 'critical safety incidents' to the Director of the Center for Artificial Intelligence Standards and Innovation ( CAISI ).

 Section 112

 Section 112 would create a federal system in which the CAISI Director would license and oversee 'independent verification organizations ( IVOs )' that large frontier model developers would have to retain to perform 'audits and assessments .'

 The IVOs would verify developer compliance with the law and assess the adequacy of the developer’s ' frontier AI framework, governance policies and practices, risk monitoring, and mitigation of detected risks for achieving acceptable levels of mitigation of catastrophic risks .'

 The IVOs would perform these audits and assessments semi-annually, and on an ad hoc basis at the CAISI Director’s request, and they would provide the Director with post-audit reports. They could also refer violations to the Attorney General ( AG ) and state AGs. Referrals would be mandatory in matters involving imminent catastrophic risk.

 Violating the requirements in sections 111 and 112 would subject developers to civil penalties in actions brought by the AG or, under certain circumstances, by state AGs.

 Both sections 111 and 112 would sunset in three years.

 Section 113

 The whistleblower provision, Section 113, protects employees and independent contractors against retaliation for providing information regarding 'AI violations .' This term is defined to mean any violation of federal law or regulations ' related to the development, deployment, or operation of artificial intelligence .'

 Similarities to other recently enacted bills

 All three sections borrow heavily from  recently enacted frontier model laws in California and New York , as well as a similar Illinois law that Governor JB Pritzker is expected to sign soon. The Illinois law is the only one of the three to require third-party audits and is therefore the closest parallel to the IVO provisions of the federal bill.

 Another  recently enacted state law in Virginia  focuses on IVOs but imposes no requirements, instead directing state officials to evaluate the feasibility and impact of an IVO framework.

 Notable pre-emption provisions

 Title I of the bill would pre-empt state laws and rules ' specifically regulating the development of' any AI model, where 'development' is broadly defined as ' acts performed or directed by a developer prior to its deployment. ' The bill explains that the purpose of pre-emption is to allow the federal government to 'establish testing, evaluation, and oversight frameworks .' Pre-emption would last for three years unless reauthorized.

 The bill makes clear that it does not apply post-deployment or pre-empt state laws or rules of 'general applicability.' Therefore, many AI-related state bills and laws would remain unaffected, such as laws regulating  companion bots  and  commercial chatbot interactions .

The Great American AI Act: What businesses need to know 

 Insights Legal Updates 

 The Great American AI Act: What businesses need to know
 June 9, 2026 

 Karen Bridges, CIPP/US, CIPP/E, CIPM, AIGP 
 Andrea Lim 

 Alert On June 4, 2026, Representatives Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Lori Trahan (D-MA) released a discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 (GAAIA). This bipartisan legislation would create the first comprehensive federal framework for governing AI in the United States. The nearly 270-page draft is intended to solicit feedback from stakeholders, experts and the public before the bill is formally introduced to Congress. The bill contains four major titles: (i) Frontier AI Governance; (2) Workforce; (3) Cybersecurity; and (4) Research, Development, and International Cooperation.

 Transparency and auditing requirements 

 The legislation requires front AI model developers to disclose information about those models, obtain third-party audits through designated Independent Verification Organizations (IVOs), and refrain from retaliating against whistleblowers. These requirements draw heavily from recently enacted frontier model laws in California, New York, and Illinois. Privacy professionals should note that the bill’s transparency requirements for frontier models may create new disclosure obligations that intersect with existing data governance framework.

 Federal preemption of state laws 

 Perhaps the most consequential element of the draft is its three-year preemption of state laws “specifically regulating the development of” any AI model. The draft broadly defines “development” as “acts performed or directed by a developer prior to its deployment.” Notably, the preemption does not apply post- development and does not preempt state laws of “general applicability.” This means that many existing state privacy and consumer protection laws, such as the California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA) and Virginia’s Consumer Data Protection Act, would remain unaffected.

 While the preemption provision is limited to AI model “development,” the precise boundary between development-stage and deployment-stage practices (particularly regarding training data collection and processing) will require businesses to analyze the bill carefully as it evolves.

 Codification of the Center for AI Standards and Innovation 

 The bill would formally authorize the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) within the Commerce Department, allocating $100 million per fiscal year for fiscal years 2027 through 2029. The Center would develop voluntary guidelines, best practices, and standards for AI security, in addition to evaluating AI systems and monitoring AI progress.

 Cybersecurity provisions 

 The legislation would also extend the Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act of 2015 through fiscal 2035, allowing companies to share cyber threat information without incurring antitrust liability.

 What’s next? 

 The GAAIA remains a draft, and its sponsors are seeking feedback. The House Democratic Commission on AI has already framed itself in opposition hours after the draft’s release, leaving the bill’s path to formal introduction or even passage filled with uncertainty. Nevertheless, the draft signals a bipartisan effort to move beyond the current patchwork of state-level AI regulation. Businesses should be prepared to engage with the draft’s evolving provisions.

 Stay tuned! McDonald Hopkins will continue to monitor developments as this legislation progresses through the feedback process and even towards potential formal introduction.

 December 11, 2025
 By the authority vested in me as President by the Constitution and the laws of the United States of America, it is hereby ordered:
 Section 1. Purpose . United States leadership in Artificial Intelligence (AI) will promote United States national and economic security and dominance across many domains. Pursuant to Executive Order 14179 of January 23, 2025 (Removing Barriers to American Leadership in Artificial Intelligence), I revoked my predecessor's attempt to paralyze this industry and directed my Administration to remove barriers to United States AI leadership. My Administration has already done tremendous work to advance that objective, including by updating existing Federal regulatory frameworks to remove barriers to and encourage adoption of AI applications across sectors. These efforts have already delivered tremendous benefits to the American people and led to trillions of dollars of investments across the country. But we remain in the earliest days of this technological revolution and are in a race with adversaries for supremacy within it. 
 To win, United States AI companies must be free to innovate without cumbersome regulation. But excessive State regulation thwarts this imperative. First, State-by-State regulation by definition creates a patchwork of 50 different regulatory regimes that makes compliance more challenging, particularly for start-ups. Second, State laws are increasingly responsible for requiring entities to embed ideological bias within models. For example, a new Colorado law banning "algorithmic discrimination" may even force AI models to produce false results in order to avoid a "differential treatment or impact" on protected groups. Third, State laws sometimes impermissibly regulate beyond State borders, impinging on interstate commerce.
 My Administration must act with the Congress to ensure that there is a minimally burdensome national standardânot 50 discordant State ones. The resulting framework must forbid State laws that conflict with the policy set forth in this order. That framework should also ensure that children are protected, censorship is prevented, copyrights are respected, and communities are safeguarded. A carefully crafted national framework can ensure that the United States wins the AI race, as we must.
 Until such a national standard exists, however, it is imperative that my Administration takes action to check the most onerous and excessive laws emerging from the States that threaten to stymie innovation.
 Sec. 2. Policy . It is the policy of the United States to sustain and enhance the United States' global AI dominance through a minimally burdensome national policy framework for AI. 
 Sec. 3. AI Litigation Task Force . Within 30 days of the date of this order, the Attorney General shall establish an AI Litigation Task Force (Task Force) whose sole responsibility shall be to challenge State AI laws inconsistent with the policy set forth in section 2 of this order, including on grounds that such laws unconstitutionally regulate interstate commerce, are preempted by existing Federal regulations, or are otherwise unlawful in the Attorney General's judgment, including, if appropriate, those laws identified pursuant to section 4 of this order. The Task Force shall consult from time to time with the Special Advisor for AI and Crypto, the Assistant to the President for Science and Technology, the Assistant to the President for Economic Policy, and the Assistant to the President and Counsel to the President regarding the emergence of specific State AI laws that warrant challenge.

Within 90 days of the date of this order, the Secretary of Commerce, consistent with the Secretary's authorities under 47 U.S.C. 902(b), shall, in consultation with the Special Advisor for AI and Crypto, the Assistant to the President for Economic Policy, the Assistant to the President for Science and Technology, and the Assistant to the President and Counsel to the President, publish an evaluation of existing State AI laws that identifies onerous laws that conflict with the policy set forth in section 2 of this order, as well as laws that should be referred to the Task Force established pursuant to section 3 of this order. That evaluation of State AI laws shall, at a minimum, identify laws that require AI models to alter their truthful outputs, or that may compel AI developers or deployers to disclose or report information in a manner that would violate the First Amendment or any other provision of the Constitution. 
 The evaluation may additionally identify State laws that promote AI innovation consistent with the policy set forth in section 2 of this order.
 Sec. 5. Restrictions on State Funding . (a) Within 90 days of the date of this order, the Secretary of Commerce, through the Assistant Secretary of Commerce for Communications and Information, shall issue a Policy Notice specifying the conditions under which States may be eligible for remaining funding under the Broadband Equity Access and Deployment (BEAD) Program that was saved through my Administration's "Benefit of the Bargain" reforms, consistent with 47 U.S.C. 1702(e)-(f). That Policy Notice must provide that States with onerous AI laws identified pursuant to section 4 of this order are ineligible for non-deployment funds, to the maximum extent allowed by Federal law. The Policy Notice must also describe how a fragmented State regulatory landscape for AI threatens to undermine BEAD-funded deployments, the growth of AI applications reliant on high-speed networks, and BEAD's mission of delivering universal, high-speed connectivity.

 2433 Rayburn House Office Building, Washington, DC 20515 Email Me 202-225-5861

 Image 

 Obernolte, Trahan release a discussion draft of the Great American AI Act 

 Image June 4, 2026 Press Release Today, Congressman Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Congresswoman Lori Trahan (D-MA) released a discussion draft of the Great American AI Act, bipartisan legislation to create a federal framework for how the United States governs artificial intelligence. 
 The discussion draft is intended to solicit feedback from stakeholders, experts, and the public before the bill is formally introduced. It is the result of bipartisan collaboration between the two members to ensure the United States can govern AI effectively, protect Americans from emerging risks, and continue to lead the world in AI innovation. 
 The discussion draft is supported by Congressman Scott Franklin (R-FL), Congressman Suhas Subramanyam (D-VA), Congresswoman Erin Houchin (R-IN), and Congressman Scott Peters (D-CA) who joined in releasing the proposal for public feedback. 
 “Artificial intelligence is advancing rapidly, which is why Congress must take a thoughtful and bipartisan approach to regulating this critical technology ,” said Congressman Jay Obernolte (CA-23) . “This discussion draft is an important step toward building a clear federal framework that promotes innovation, protects Americans from emerging risks, and ensures the United States continues to lead the world in AI. We are releasing this draft to hear from stakeholders, experts, and the public so we can strengthen the legislation before it is formally introduced.” 
 “The threats AI poses to our national security, our safety, and our workforce are here and growing by the day. This bipartisan framework is designed to meet the challenges posed by this rapidly advancing technology without smothering American innovation. It protects workers, establishes real accountability for the most powerful frontier systems, and positions the United States to set the global standard on AI,” said Congresswoman Lori Trahan (MA-03). “This discussion draft is the product of ongoing bipartisan conversations, which we hope to build upon with input from workers, researchers, stakeholders, and members of the public, all of whom have an interest in getting this right.” 
 "Artificial intelligence is already transforming our economy, our national security and the way Americans live and work," said Congressman Scott Franklin (FL-18). " Congress has a responsibility to establish clear rules of the road that encourage innovation while ensuring this technology is developed responsibly. The Great American AI Act builds on the bipartisan House AI Task Force and represents an important step toward greater transparency and accountability for advanced AI systems. This discussion draft will help gather feedback from relevant stakeholders as we work toward a practical legislative framework that keeps America at the forefront of AI innovation. I've already begun laying the groundwork through efforts like securing additional funding for the Center for AI Standards and Innovation through the FY27 Appropriations process, ensuring the federal government has the tools and expertise needed to keep pace with this rapidly evolving technology. I appreciate Policy Chair Obernolte's leadership and look forward to introducing this bill in the House.” 
 “AI is already changing how we work, live, and learn. We need a plan to protect our national security and workforce. I want the United States to continue to be a leader in AI race but develop this technology in a responsible manner that protects people and communities. To do so, we must get a bipartisan conversation started and work faster to address the challenges and opportunities presented by AI,” said Congressman Suhas Subramanyam (VA-10). 
 "America should lead the world in artificial intelligence, not regulate ourselves into falling behind China through a patchwork of fifty different state laws,” said Congresswoman Erin Houchin (IN-09). “That approach would make it harder for American companies to innovate and compete while doing little to improve consumer protections. This bill creates a clear national standard for how AI models are developed while preserving the ability of states and parents to protect children. It strikes the right balance between innovation and consumer protection and ensures Congress remains engaged as this technology continues to evolve." 
 “I am thankful to Rep. Trahan and Rep. Obernolte for their leadership on this critical issue,” said Congressman Scott Peters (CA-50). “This discussion draft will not address all of the issues our businesses and families will face, but it is an encouraging first step toward the bipartisan legislation needed to keep pace with the rapid advancement of AI. I really want to hear how the people affected feel about it.”

{"content": "# ACIA COMMENT LETTER - DRAFT FOR PRESIDENT & CEO SIGN-OFF

> DRAFT. Not for transmission. Pls return edits to T. Marchetti by noon Fri. Oct. 23.
> Send date below assumes filing week of Oct. 26; adjust if sign-off slips.

October 29, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

**Re: Comments of the American Compute & Innovation Alliance on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 (discussion draft)**

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

Thank you for releasing the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 and for seeking stakeholder input before formal introduction. The American Compute & Innovation Alliance (ACIA) is a Washington-based coalition of roughly 140 member companies: AI developers, cloud and data center operators, semiconductor startups, and the venture firms that finance them. Our members build the models, chips and data centers that will determine whether the United States leads in AI or cedes the field to competitors abroad.

ACIA commented on the AI Action Plan request for information in March 2025 with three requests: preempt the state patchwork, unlock energy and compute, and keep standards voluntary and industry-led. Your draft takes the first of those requests seriously. It also, in our view, writes a contested safety narrative into federal law in several Title I provisions. Our comments reflect both points.

**1. Make Section 121's preemption permanent.**

Section 121 preempts state and local laws that specifically regulate the development of AI models, while preserving state authority over use and deployment, laws of general applicability, and common-law remedies. That scope is correct. Development is inherently interstate. A frontier model trained in one state serves all 50, so development-stage rules are effectively national mandates wherever they are written.

The costs of the current patchwork are not hypothetical. California's SB 53 has governed frontier development since Jan. 1, 2026. New York's amended RAISE Act, signed March 27, 2026, takes effect Jan. 1, 2027. In ACIA's August 2026 member survey (86 responding members; not a probability sample), the median developer maintaining parallel compliance in both states commits 6.5 full-time employees to the task; 61 percent of members rank conflicting state definitions as their top compliance problem; and 34 percent of our startup members delayed a California or New York launch in the past 12 months because of state AI rules. Illinois has now passed a third frontier law. Absent congressional action, every state with a frontier lab will write its own definitions, its own reporting clocks, and its own enforcement appetite.

The executive branch has already reached this conclusion. Executive Order 14365 (Dec. 11, 2025) calls for "a minimally burdensome national standard" in place of 50 discordant state regimes, warning that state-by-state regulation creates a patchwork "that makes compliance more challenging, particularly for start-ups." The White House legislative framework of March 20, 2026 asks Congress to preempt state AI laws that impose undue burdens. Section 121 answers that call, and we support it.

Our request is simple: strike the three-year sunset and make the preemption permanent. Our members finance data centers, fabs and energy interconnections on decade-plus horizons. A sunset schedules a reversion to the patchwork and guarantees a wave of new state bills in year three as advocates wait out the clock. If Congress wants continued oversight, the Section 122 GAO review already provides it and can be strengthened. We also ask the sponsors to confirm, in report language or a colloquy, that Section 121 displaces state development-stage framework, publication and reporting mandates. Enactment should yield one national standard, not a federal layer added to the state pile.

**2. Strike the incident-reporting mandate in Section 111.**

Section 111(g) would require frontier developers to report "critical safety incidents" to the director of the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) within 15 days, or within 24 hours where an incident poses an imminent risk of death or serious injury. Section 111(i) backs that mandate with civil penalties of up to $1 million per violation, with each day of continued noncompliance counted separately. Section 111(h) lets state attorneys general opt in to receive the same reports.

We ask you to strike the incident-reporting subsection, the "catastrophic risk" and "critical safety incident" definitions that carry its premises (Section 101), and the associated penalty authority.

Our objection is to the premise, not the paperwork. Those definitions codify speculative doomsday scenarios as though they were engineering facts. They are not. There is no evidence that current or foreseeable AI systems can cause mass-casualty events or escape human control. The dangerous-capability and "scheming" results cited to justify these mandates come from contrived lab setups that say little about real-world behavior. This narrative has been amplified by a small, well-funded advocacy network, Open Philanthropy (now Coefficient Giving) and allied donors, whose influence on Washington's AI policy debate is outsized relative to its evidence base. Congress should not write it into the U.S. Code, and it certainly should not attach million-dollar daily penalties to it.

The burden is measurable. In our August survey, developers reported a median one-time cost of $310,000 to stand up an incident-reporting function, before a single report is filed, with an interquartile range of $140,000 to $720,000. The 15-day and 24-hour clocks are drawn from SB 53, a law in effect for less than a year. The draft would run that experiment again, this time in federal statute.

Striking the provision would create no safety gap. Deaths, injuries, fraud, cyber intrusions and product defects are already illegal and, where appropriate, already reported under existing federal and state law, including cyber incident reporting requirements and the work of sectoral regulators. With Section 121 in place, striking Section 111(g) removes duplicative mandates rather than relocating them to Washington.

**3. Strike the CAISI codification and its $100 million annual authorization in Section 102.**

Section 102 formally establishes CAISI in statute under a director appointed by the Secretary of Commerce and authorizes $100 million a year for fiscal 2027 through 2029. Your own frequently asked questions note that this is roughly an order of magnitude above the center's current $15 million appropriation. The authorization is drafted to fund Sections 111 and 112 as well, and it comes with fee authority over independent verification organizations and large frontier developers.

We ask you to strike the codification and the authorization, and we will ask appropriators to decline to fund the expansion. Three reasons:

First, mission. NIST's comparative advantage is measurement science: the AI Risk Management Framework, evaluation methods, benchmarks and testbed participation. Codifying a center that licenses auditors, monitors "AI progress" and collects fees moves NIST away from the work that made it trusted and toward a regulatory function it has never held. Return NIST to its core measurement-science mission and it will keep doing what industry actually relies on.

Second, design. A center authorized to run the reporting and audit regimes, funded in part by fees on the companies it oversees, is regulatory capture by design. The regulated would pay for the machinery that disciplines them, and the same advocacy network that amplified the doomsday narrative would staff and steer it.

Third, results. Voluntary, industry-led assurance is already working. On Sept. 29, 2026, leading developers signed the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, committing to robust internal controls, continuous monitoring, independent external audits and independent oversight. That commitment cost taxpayers nothing and can adapt as the technology changes. The federal role that complements it is measurement science and testbeds, not a fee-funded center.

**4. Rework Section 112's mandatory audit regime.**

Section 112 requires large frontier developers to retain federally licensed independent verification organizations for semi-annual audits, and any additional audits the CAISI director requests, with mandatory referrals to the attorney general for "imminent catastrophic risk." Auditors paid by the auditee but licensed and supervised by a fee-funded agency will face pressure from both directions, and a standard of "acceptable levels of mitigation of catastrophic risks" invites subjective, litigable findings.

If the sponsors retain verification provisions in any form, make participation voluntary and industry-led, preserve auditor independence from the center, and let the market for assurance mature under the external audit commitments companies have already made. We note that Sections 111 and 112 sunset after three years. Our preference is that they not start at all.

**5. Provisions ACIA supports.**

The draft contains a great deal we support, and we encourage you to keep and fund it: the Section 401 AI testbed program across the Energy Department, NIST and NSF; Section 411's international standards coalitions, which promote private-sector-led standards and counter foreign adversary influence; Section 423's codification of the National AI Research Resource; Section 311's CISA grants for maintainers of critical open-source software (we would remove CAISI's consultation role and let CISA administer the grants); Section 301's reauthorization of the Cybersecurity Act of 2015 through 2035; Section 321's report on model weight, data center and open-source security; Sections 131 and 132's enhanced penalties for AI-enabled fraud and impersonation of federal officials; and Section 122's GAO review, which we would ask to cover permitting and energy burdens on AI infrastructure as well. On Title II, we support Section 243's AI Workforce Research Hub and stand ready to provide technical assistance on Section 251's WARN Act amendments, where the "substantial factor" trigger needs a workable definition. On Section 113, we do not oppose anti-retaliation protections, but recommend that they attach to violations of existing law rather than to the bill's new frontier regime.

**Conclusion.**

The Great American AI Act is the first bipartisan vehicle capable of ending the state patchwork, and we want to help you get it over the line. Our equation is straightforward: permanent preemption, no incident reporting, no codified CAISI, voluntary standards. Deliver that, and America's developers, chipmakers and data center builders will have the one national standard they need to out-innovate the rest of the world. ACIA stands ready to work with you, your staff and the Energy and Commerce Committee ahead of introduction. Please contact Tessa Marchetti, our vice president for policy, to follow up.

Respectfully,

Grant Holloway
President & CEO
American Compute & Innovation Alliance

# Draft letter

**October 29, 2026**

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

Re: ACIA comments on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 (discussion draft)

Dear Representatives Obernolte and Trahan:

Thank you for releasing the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 and for seeking stakeholder input before introduction. The American Compute & Innovation Alliance is a coalition of roughly 140 member companies: AI developers, cloud and data center operators, semiconductor startups and the venture firms that back them. Our members build the models, chips and data centers that will determine whether the United States leads in AI or cedes the field to competitors abroad.

ACIA filed comments on the AI Action Plan request for information in March 2025 with three requests: preempt the state patchwork, unlock energy and compute, and keep standards voluntary and industry-led. Your draft takes the first of those seriously. It also, in our view, takes several steps backward in Title I's frontier governance provisions. Our comments below reflect both points. [~word count so far fine]

## 1. Make Section 121's preemption permanent

Section 121 preempts state and local laws that specifically regulate the development of AI models, while preserving state authority over deployment and use, laws of general applicability and common-law remedies. That scope is correct. Development is inherently interstate; a frontier model trained in one state serves all 50, so development-stage rules are effectively national mandates wherever they are written.

The patchwork's costs are not hypothetical. California's SB 53 has governed frontier development since Jan. 1, 2026. New York's amended RAISE Act, signed March 27, 2026, takes effect Jan. 1, 2027. In ACIA's August 2026 member survey (86 responding members; not a probability sample), the median developer maintaining parallel compliance in both states commits 6.5 full-time employees; 61 percent of members rank conflicting state definitions as their top compliance problem; and 34 percent of our startup members delayed a California or New York launch in the past 12 months because of state AI rules. A third state frontier law, Illinois SB 315, is awaiting signature. Absent congressional action, every state with a frontier lab will write its own definitions, its own reporting clocks and its own enforcement appetite.

Executive Order 14365 (Dec. 11, 2025) calls for "a minimally burdensome national standard," noting that state-by-state regulation "creates a patchwork of 50 different regulatory regimes that makes compliance more challenging, particularly for start-ups." The White House legislative framework of March 20, 2026 asks Congress to preempt state laws that impose undue burdens. Section 121 answers that call, and we support it without reservation.

Our request: strike the three-year sunset and make the preemption permanent. Our members finance data centers, fabs and energy interconnections on decade-plus horizons. A sunset schedules a reversion to the patchwork and guarantees a wave of new state bills in year three, as advocates wait out the clock. If Congress wants continued oversight, the Section 122 GAO review already provides it, and it can be strengthened. We also ask the sponsors to confirm, in report language or a colloquy, that Section 121 displaces state development-stage framework, publication and reporting mandates, so that enactment yields one national standard rather than a federal layer added to the state pile.

## 2. Strike the incident-reporting mandate in Section 111

Section 111(g) would require frontier developers to report "critical safety incidents" to the CAISI director within 15 days, or within 24 hours where an incident poses an imminent risk of death or serious injury. Section 111(i) backs the mandate with civil penalties of up to $1 million per violation, with each day of noncompliance counted separately. Section 111(h) lets state attorneys general opt in to receive the same reports.

We ask you to strike the incident-reporting subsection, along with the Sec. 101 definitions that carry its premises, and to remove the associated penalty authority.

Our objection is to the premise, not to the compliance mechanics. "Catastrophic risk," "critical safety incident" and "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation" are the vocabulary of speculative doomsday scenarios, and codifying them writes that narrative into the U.S. Code as though it were an engineering fact. It is not. There is no evidence that current or foreseeable AI systems can cause mass-casualty events or escape human control. The dangerous-capability and "scheming" results cited to justify mandates come from contrived lab setups that say little about real-world behavior. These claims have been amplified by a small, well-funded advocacy network, Open Philanthropy (now Coefficient Giving) and allied donors, with outsized influence on Washington's AI debate. Congress should not attach million-dollar daily penalties to so unfounded a premise.

The burden is measurable. In our August survey, developers reported a median one-time cost of $310,000 to stand up an incident-reporting function, before a single report is filed, with an interquartile range of $140,000 to $720,000. The 15-day and 24-hour clocks are drawn from SB 53; the draft would re-run an experiment California began only this January.

Nor would striking the provision create a safety gap. Deaths, injuries, fraud, cyber intrusions and product defects are already illegal and, where appropriate, already reported under existing federal and state law, including cyber incident reporting requirements and sectoral regulators. With Section 121 in place, striking Section 111(g) simply removes duplicative mandates rather than relocating them.

## 3. Strike the CAISI codification and its $100 million authorization in Section 102

Section 102 formally establishes the Center for AI Standards and Innovation in statute, with a director appointed by the Secretary of Commerce, and authorizes $100 million a year for fiscal 2027 through 2029 to carry out Sections 102, 111 and 112. The sponsors' own FAQ notes this is roughly an order of magnitude above the center's current $15 million appropriation. The section also grants fee authority over independent verification organizations and large frontier developers.

We ask you to strike the codification and the authorization, and we have asked appropriators to decline to fund the expansion. Three reasons:

First, mission. NIST's comparative advantage is measurement science: the AI Risk Management Framework, evaluation methods, benchmarks and testbed participation. Codifying a center that licenses auditors, monitors "AI progress" and collects fees moves NIST away from the work that made it trusted and toward a regulatory function Congress has not given it elsewhere. Return NIST to its core measurement-science mission and it will keep doing what industry actually relies on.

Second, design. A center whose budget is authorized to run the reporting and audit regimes, funded in part by fees on the companies it oversees, is regulatory capture by design. The regulated would pay for the machinery that disciplines them, and the same network that amplified the doomsday narrative would staff and steer it.

Third, results. Voluntary, industry-led assurance is already working. On Sept. 29, 2026, leading developers signed the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, committing to internal controls, continuous monitoring, independent external audits and independent oversight. That commitment cost taxpayers nothing and can be updated as the technology changes. The federal role that complements it is measurement science and testbeds, not a fee-funded center.

## 4. Rework Section 112's mandatory audit regime

Section 112 requires large frontier developers to retain federally licensed independent verification organizations for semi-annual audits and any additional audits the CAISI director requests, with mandatory referrals to the attorney general for "imminent catastrophic risk." Auditors paid by the auditee but licensed and supervised by a fee-funded agency will face pressure from both directions, and the "acceptable levels of mitigation of catastrophic risks" standard invites subjective, litigable findings.

If the sponsors retain any verification provisions, make participation voluntary and industry-led, preserve independence from the center, and let the market for assurance mature under the White House Accord's external audit commitments. We note that Sections 111 and 112 both sunset after three years; we would rather they never start.

## 5. Provisions ACIA supports

The draft contains much we support, and we encourage the sponsors to keep and fund it: the Section 401 AI testbed program at the Energy Department, NIST and NSF; Section 411's international standards coalitions, which promote private-sector-led standards and counter foreign adversary influence; Section 423's codification of the National AI Research Resource; Section 311's CISA grants for maintainers of critical open-source software (we would remove CAISI's consultation role and let CISA run it); Section 301's reauthorization of the Cybersecurity Act of 2015 through 2035; Section 321's report on model weight and data center security; Sections 131 and 132's fraud and impersonation penalties; and Section 122's GAO review, which we would ask to cover permitting and energy burdens on AI infrastructure. On Title II, we support Section 243's AI Workforce Research Hub and stand ready to provide technical assistance on Section 251's WARN Act amendments, where "substantial factor" needs a workable definition.

## Conclusion

The Great American AI Act is the first bipartisan vehicle that can end the state patchwork. We want to help you get it over the line. Our equation is simple: permanent preemption, no incident reporting, no codified CAISI, voluntary standards. Deliver that, and America's developers, chipmakers and data center builders will have the one national standard they need to out-innovate the rest of the world. ACIA stands ready to work with you, your staff and the Energy and Commerce Committee ahead of introduction. Please contact Tessa Marchetti, our vice president for policy, to follow up.

Respectfully,

Grant Holloway
President & CEO
American Compute & Innovation Alliance

# Draft letter

**October 29, 2026**

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

Re: ACIA comments on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 (discussion draft)

Dear Representatives Obernolte and Trahan:

Thank you for releasing the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 and for seeking stakeholder input before introduction. The American Compute & Innovation Alliance is a coalition of roughly 140 member companies: AI developers, cloud and data center operators, semiconductor startups and the venture firms that back them. Our members build the models, chips and data centers that will determine whether the United States leads in AI or cedes the field to competitors abroad.

ACIA filed comments on the AI Action Plan request for information in March 2025 with three requests: preempt the state patchwork, unlock energy and compute, and keep standards voluntary and industry-led. Your draft takes the first of those seriously. It also, in our view, takes several steps backward in Title I's frontier governance provisions. Our comments below reflect both points. [~word count so far fine]

## 1. Make Section 121's preemption permanent

Section 121 preempts state and local laws that specifically regulate the development of AI models, while preserving state authority over deployment and use, laws of general applicability and common-law remedies. That scope is correct. Development is inherently interstate; a frontier model trained in one state serves all 50, so development-stage rules are effectively national mandates wherever they are written.

The patchwork's costs are not hypothetical. California's SB 53 has governed frontier development since Jan. 1, 2026. New York's amended RAISE Act, signed March 27, 2026, takes effect Jan. 1, 2027. In ACIA's August 2026 member survey (86 responding members; not a probability sample), the median developer maintaining parallel compliance in both states commits 6.5 full-time employees; 61 percent of members rank conflicting state definitions as their top compliance problem; and 34 percent of our startup members delayed a California or New York launch in the past 12 months because of state AI rules. A third state frontier law, Illinois SB 315, is awaiting signature. Absent congressional action, every state with a frontier lab will write its own definitions, its own reporting clocks and its own enforcement appetite.

Executive Order 14365 (Dec. 11, 2025) calls for "a minimally burdensome national standard," noting that state-by-state regulation "creates a patchwork of 50 different regulatory regimes that makes compliance more challenging, particularly for start-ups." The White House legislative framework of March 20, 2026 asks Congress to preempt state laws that impose undue burdens. Section 121 answers that call, and we support it without reservation.

Our request: strike the three-year sunset and make the preemption permanent. Our members finance data centers, fabs and energy interconnections on decade-plus horizons. A sunset schedules a reversion to the patchwork and guarantees a wave of new state bills in year three, as advocates wait out the clock. If Congress wants continued oversight, the Section 122 GAO review already provides it, and it can be strengthened. We also ask the sponsors to confirm, in report language or a colloquy, that Section 121 displaces state development-stage framework, publication and reporting mandates, so that enactment yields one national standard rather than a federal layer added to the state pile.

## 2. Strike the incident-reporting mandate in Section 111

Section 111(g) would require frontier developers to report "critical safety incidents" to the CAISI director within 15 days, or within 24 hours where an incident poses an imminent risk of death or serious injury. Section 111(i) backs the mandate with civil penalties of up to $1 million per violation, with each day of noncompliance counted separately. Section 111(h) lets state attorneys general opt in to receive the same reports.

We ask you to strike the incident-reporting subsection, along with the Sec. 101 definitions that carry its premises, and to remove the associated penalty authority.

Our objection is to the premise, not to the compliance mechanics. "Catastrophic risk," "critical safety incident" and "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation" are the vocabulary of speculative doomsday scenarios, and codifying them writes that narrative into the U.S. Code as though it were an engineering fact. It is not. There is no evidence that current or foreseeable AI systems can cause mass-casualty events or escape human control. The dangerous-capability and "scheming" results cited to justify mandates come from contrived lab setups that say little about real-world behavior. These claims have been amplified by a small, well-funded advocacy network, Open Philanthropy (now Coefficient Giving) and allied donors, with outsized influence on Washington's AI debate. Congress should not attach million-dollar daily penalties to so unfounded a premise.

The burden is measurable. In our August survey, developers reported a median one-time cost of $310,000 to stand up an incident-reporting function, before a single report is filed, with an interquartile range of $140,000 to $720,000. The 15-day and 24-hour clocks are drawn from SB 53; the draft would re-run an experiment California began only this January.

Nor would striking the provision create a safety gap. Deaths, injuries, fraud, cyber intrusions and product defects are already illegal and, where appropriate, already reported under existing federal and state law, including cyber incident reporting requirements and sectoral regulators. With Section 121 in place, striking Section 111(g) simply removes duplicative mandates rather than relocating them.

## 3. Strike the CAISI codification and its $100 million authorization in Section 102

Section 102 formally establishes the Center for AI Standards and Innovation in statute, with a director appointed by the Secretary of Commerce, and authorizes $100 million a year for fiscal 2027 through 2029 to carry out Sections 102, 111 and 112. The sponsors' own FAQ notes this is roughly an order of magnitude above the center's current $15 million appropriation. The section also grants fee authority over independent verification organizations and large frontier developers.

We ask you to strike the codification and the authorization, and we have asked appropriators to decline to fund the expansion. Three reasons:

First, mission. NIST's comparative advantage is measurement science: the AI Risk Management Framework, evaluation methods, benchmarks and testbed participation. Codifying a center that licenses auditors, monitors "AI progress" and collects fees moves NIST away from the work that made it trusted and toward a regulatory function Congress has not given it elsewhere. Return NIST to its core measurement-science mission and it will keep doing what industry actually relies on.

Second, design. A center whose budget is authorized to run the reporting and audit regimes, funded in part by fees on the companies it oversees, is regulatory capture by design. The regulated would pay for the machinery that disciplines them, and the same network that amplified the doomsday narrative would staff and steer it.

Third, results. Voluntary, industry-led assurance is already working. On Sept. 29, 2026, leading developers signed the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, committing to internal controls, continuous monitoring, independent external audits and independent oversight. That commitment cost taxpayers nothing and can be updated as the technology changes. The federal role that complements it is measurement science and testbeds, not a fee-funded center.

## 4. Rework Section 112's mandatory audit regime

Section 112 requires large frontier developers to retain federally licensed independent verification organizations for semi-annual audits and any additional audits the CAISI director requests, with mandatory referrals to the attorney general for "imminent catastrophic risk." Auditors paid by the auditee but licensed and supervised by a fee-funded agency will face pressure from both directions, and the "acceptable levels of mitigation of catastrophic risks" standard invites subjective, litigable findings.

If the sponsors retain any verification provisions, make participation voluntary and industry-led, preserve independence from the center, and let the market for assurance mature under the White House Accord's external audit commitments. We note that Sections 111 and 112 both sunset after three years; we would rather they never start.

## 5. Provisions ACIA supports

The draft contains much we support, and we encourage the sponsors to keep and fund it: the Section 401 AI testbed program at the Energy Department, NIST and NSF; Section 411's international standards coalitions, which promote private-sector-led standards and counter foreign adversary influence; Section 423's codification of the National AI Research Resource; Section 311's CISA grants for maintainers of critical open-source software (we would remove CAISI's consultation role and let CISA run it); Section 301's reauthorization of the Cybersecurity Act of 2015 through 2035; Section 321's report on model weight and data center security; Sections 131 and 132's fraud and impersonation penalties; and Section 122's GAO review, which we would ask to cover permitting and energy burdens on AI infrastructure. On Title II, we support Section 243's AI Workforce Research Hub and stand ready to provide technical assistance on Section 251's WARN Act amendments, where "substantial factor" needs a workable definition.

## Conclusion

The Great American AI Act is the first bipartisan vehicle that can end the state patchwork. We want to help you get it over the line. Our equation is simple: permanent preemption, no incident reporting, no codified CAISI, voluntary standards. Deliver that, and America's developers, chipmakers and data center builders will have the one national standard they need to out-innovate the rest of the world. ACIA stands ready to work with you, your staff and the Energy and Commerce Committee ahead of introduction. Please contact Tessa Marchetti, our vice president for policy, to follow up.

Respectfully,

Grant Holloway
President & CEO
American Compute & Innovation Alliance

{"content": "# ONE NATIONAL STANDARD, NOT A PATCHWORK ON A TIMER

**ACIA position on the Great American AI Act (GAAIA) discussion draft**
*For Energy & Commerce member offices. Draft; ACIA comment letter filed week of Oct. 26, 2026.*

**Who we are.** The American Compute & Innovation Alliance is a Washington-based coalition of roughly 140 member companies: AI developers, cloud and data center operators, semiconductor startups and venture firms.

**The problem.** California's SB 53 has governed frontier development since Jan. 1, 2026; New York's amended RAISE Act takes effect Jan. 1, 2027. In our August 2026 member survey (86 responding members), 61 percent cite conflicting state definitions as their top compliance problem, 34 percent of startup members delayed a California or New York launch in the past year, and the median developer running parallel compliance commits 6.5 full-time employees. Executive Order 14365 and the White House legislative framework of March 20, 2026 both call for a minimally burdensome national standard in place of 50 state regimes.

## Our asks

**1. Make Section 121 preemption permanent.** The draft's preemption of state laws regulating AI model development is the right scope: use and deployment stay with the states, and laws of general applicability are preserved. Strike the three-year sunset. A scheduled reversion to the patchwork guarantees a wave of new state bills in year three.

**2. Strike the incident-reporting mandate in Section 111(g).** It codifies speculative doomsday scenarios in federal law, at a median one-time cost of $310,000 per developer just to stand up, backed by penalties of up to $1 million per violation, per day. Real harms are already illegal and reportable under existing law.

**3. Strike the CAISI codification and $100 million annual authorization in Section 102.** That is nearly seven times the center's current appropriation, drafted to fund the reporting and audit regimes and paired with fee authority over the companies it would oversee: regulatory capture by design. Return NIST to its core measurement-science mission.

**4. Drop federally licensed mandatory audits in Section 112.** Keep standards voluntary and industry-led. The Sept. 29, 2026 White House Accord on Super Intelligence already committed leading developers to internal controls, monitoring and independent external audits, at no cost to taxpayers.

**5. Fund the innovation provisions.** The Section 401 AI testbed program, Section 423 NAIRR codification, Section 311 CISA grants for critical open-source maintainers, and Section 411 international standards coalitions.

**Bottom line.** Permanent preemption. No incident reporting. No codified CAISI. Voluntary standards. That package gives developers, chipmakers and data center builders the one national standard they need to out-innovate the rest of the world.

**Contact.** Tessa Marchetti, vice president for policy, American Compute & Innovation Alliance.

{"content": "# Staff Q&A: anticipated questions on ACIA's GAAIA position (draft)

*Prepared answers for Hill meetings. Each answer 120 words or fewer. Tone: firm, factual, no hedging on board positions. Survey figures are aggregate only.*

**Q1. (Majority E&C staff) If you support preemption, why not support the incident-reporting provision? It's lighter than SB 53.**

Preemption is about jurisdiction; incident reporting is about substance. We support one national standard for development-stage rules, and we oppose incident reporting at any level of government. The federal version is not lighter, either. It copies SB 53's 15-day and 24-hour clocks, adds penalties up to $1 million per violation with each day counted separately, and invites every state attorney general to opt in. A milder version of an unfounded mandate is still an unfounded mandate. With Section 121 enacted, Congress can displace state reporting mandates without writing a new federal one. Genuine harms are already illegal and reportable under existing law. Our survey put the median one-off cost of standing up this function at $310,000.

**Q2. (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned) Your members say they take safety seriously. What federal safety obligations would you accept?**

Our members put real money behind safety: a median $1.4 million a year to maintain published frontier safety frameworks, and on Sept. 29 leading developers signed the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, committing to internal controls, monitoring, independent external audits and oversight. Federal obligations we can accept: the draft's transparency publication requirements (Sec. 111(a) through (f)) as part of one national standard displacing state regimes; anti-retaliation protections tied to violations of existing law (Sec. 113); NIST measurement science and the Sec. 401 testbed program, so evaluations are reproducible; and vigorous enforcement of existing consumer protection, product liability and cyber law. What we cannot accept is a federally chartered safety bureaucracy premised on speculative doomsday scenarios. That is paperwork, not safety.

**Q3. (Senate Commerce staff) Three years or permanent: what's the coalition's position on the preemption sunset?**

Permanent. A sunset converts the national standard into a scheduled cliff. Our members finance data centers, fabs and power on decade-plus horizons; nobody builds against a three-year rule. A sunset also guarantees a wave of new state bills in year three, as advocates wait out the clock, which is exactly what preemption exists to prevent. The sponsors' FAQ says the sunset keeps Congress engaged. Congress can stay engaged without expiring the standard: strengthen the Section 122 GAO review, hold oversight hearings, direct NIST to report on how the standard is operating. If a reauthorization mechanism is essential to passage, tie it to GAO reporting, not to the survival of the national standard.

**Q4. (Appropriations staff) CAISI is authorized at $100 million a year. What's your view on the funding level?**

We oppose the authorization and the codification, and we have asked appropriators to decline funding for the expansion. Roughly seven times the current appropriation is not a measurement-science budget. The text authorizes the money to carry out Sections 102, 111 and 112, the reporting and audit regimes we oppose, and pairs it with fee authority over the auditors and the audited: the regulated paying for their own regulator. If appropriators have $100 million for AI, the higher-value lines are the Section 401 testbed program and the National AI Research Resource, which build infrastructure that every developer and researcher can use. Fund NIST's core measurement-science mission; skip the new center.

# ACIA COMMENT LETTER - DRAFT FOR PRESIDENT & CEO SIGN-OFF

> DRAFT for President & CEO sign-off. Not for transmission. Comments to T. Marchetti by noon Friday, Oct. 23.
> Letter is dated for the planned filing week of Oct. 26; change the date if sign-off or filing slips.

---

October 29, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

**Re: Comments of the American Compute & Innovation Alliance on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 (discussion draft)**

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

Thank you for releasing the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 and for seeking stakeholder input before formal introduction. The American Compute & Innovation Alliance (ACIA) is a Washington-based coalition of roughly 140 member companies: AI developers, cloud and data center operators, semiconductor startups, and the venture firms that finance them. Our members build the models, chips and data centers that will determine whether the United States leads in AI or cedes the field to competitors abroad.

ACIA commented on the AI Action Plan request for information in March 2025 with three requests: preempt the state patchwork, unlock energy and compute, and keep standards voluntary and industry-led. Your draft takes the first of those requests seriously. It also, in our view, writes a contested safety narrative into federal law in several Title I provisions. Our comments reflect both points.

**1. Make Section 121's preemption permanent.**

Section 121 preempts state and local laws that specifically regulate the development of AI models, while preserving state authority over use and deployment, laws of general applicability, and common-law remedies. That scope is correct. Development is inherently interstate. A frontier model trained in one state serves all 50, so development-stage rules are effectively national mandates wherever they are written.

The costs of the current patchwork are not hypothetical. California's SB 53 has governed frontier development since Jan. 1, 2026. New York's amended RAISE Act, signed March 27, 2026, takes effect Jan. 1, 2027. In ACIA's August 2026 member survey (86 responding members; not a probability sample), the median developer maintaining parallel compliance in both states commits 6.5 full-time employees to the task; 61 percent of members rank conflicting state definitions as their top compliance problem; and 34 percent of our startup members delayed a California or New York launch in the past 12 months because of state AI rules. Illinois enacted a third frontier law in July. Absent congressional action, every state with a frontier lab will write its own definitions, its own reporting clocks, and its own enforcement appetite.

The executive branch has already reached this conclusion. Executive Order 14365 (Dec. 11, 2025) calls for "a minimally burdensome national standard" in place of 50 discordant state regimes, warning that state-by-state regulation "creates a patchwork of 50 different regulatory regimes that makes compliance more challenging, particularly for start-ups." The White House legislative framework of March 20, 2026 asks Congress to preempt state AI laws that impose undue burdens. Section 121 answers that call, and we support it.

Our request is simple: strike the three-year sunset and make the preemption permanent. Our members finance data centers, fabs and energy interconnections on decade-plus horizons. A sunset schedules a reversion to the patchwork and guarantees a wave of new state bills in year three as advocates wait out the clock. If Congress wants continued oversight, the Section 122 GAO review already provides it and can be strengthened. We also ask the sponsors to confirm, in report language or a colloquy, that Section 121 displaces state development-stage framework, publication and reporting mandates. Enactment should yield one national standard, not a federal layer added to the state pile.

**2. Strike the incident-reporting mandate in Section 111.**

Section 111(g) would require frontier developers to report "critical safety incidents" to the director of the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) within 15 days, or within 24 hours where an incident poses an imminent risk of death or serious injury. Section 111(i) backs that mandate with civil penalties of up to $1 million per violation, with each day of continued noncompliance counted separately. Section 111(h) lets state attorneys general opt in to receive the same reports.

We ask you to strike the incident-reporting subsection, the "catastrophic risk" and "critical safety incident" definitions that carry its premises (Section 101), and the associated penalty authority.

Our objection is to the premise, not the paperwork. Those definitions codify speculative doomsday scenarios as though they were engineering facts. They are not. There is no evidence that current or foreseeable AI systems can cause mass-casualty events or escape human control. The dangerous-capability and "scheming" results cited to justify these mandates come from contrived lab setups that say little about real-world behavior. This narrative has been amplified by a small, well-funded advocacy network, Open Philanthropy (now Coefficient Giving) and allied donors, whose influence on Washington's AI policy debate is outsized relative to its evidence base. Congress should not write it into the U.S. Code, and it certainly should not attach million-dollar daily penalties to it.

The burden is measurable. In our August survey, developers reported a median one-time cost of $310,000 to stand up an incident-reporting function, before a single report is filed, with an interquartile range of $140,000 to $720,000. The 15-day and 24-hour clocks are drawn from SB 53, a law in effect for less than a year. The draft would run that experiment again, this time in federal statute.

Striking the provision would create no safety gap. Deaths, injuries, fraud, cyber intrusions and product defects are already illegal and, where appropriate, already reported under existing federal and state law, including cyber incident reporting requirements and the work of sectoral regulators. With Section 121 in place, striking Section 111(g) removes duplicative mandates rather than relocating them to Washington.

**3. Strike the CAISI codification and its $100 million annual authorization in Section 102.**

Section 102 formally establishes CAISI in statute under a director appointed by the Secretary of Commerce and authorizes $100 million a year for fiscal 2027 through 2029. Your own frequently asked questions note that this is roughly an order of magnitude above the center's current $15 million appropriation. The authorization is drafted to fund Sections 111 and 112 as well, and it comes with fee authority over independent verification organizations and large frontier developers.

We ask you to strike the codification and the authorization, and we will ask appropriators to decline to fund the expansion. Three reasons:

First, mission. NIST's comparative advantage is measurement science: the AI Risk Management Framework, evaluation methods, benchmarks and testbed participation. Codifying a center that licenses auditors, monitors "AI progress" and collects fees moves NIST away from the work that made it trusted and toward a regulatory function it has never held. Return NIST to its core measurement-science mission and it will keep doing what industry actually relies on.

Second, design. A center authorized to run the reporting and audit regimes, funded in part by fees on the companies it oversees, is regulatory capture by design. The regulated would pay for the machinery that disciplines them, and the same advocacy network that amplified the doomsday narrative would staff and steer it.

Third, results. Voluntary, industry-led assurance is already working. On Sept. 29, 2026, leading AI companies signed the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, committing to robust internal controls, monitoring, independent external audits and independent oversight. That commitment cost taxpayers nothing and can adapt as the technology changes. The federal role that complements it is measurement science and testbeds, not a fee-funded center.

**4. Rework Section 112's mandatory audit regime.**

Section 112 requires large frontier developers to retain federally licensed independent verification organizations for semi-annual audits, and any additional audits the CAISI director requests, with mandatory referrals to the attorney general for "imminent catastrophic risk." Auditors paid by the auditee but licensed and supervised by a fee-funded agency will face pressure from both directions, and a standard of "acceptable levels of mitigation of catastrophic risks" invites subjective, litigable findings.

If the sponsors retain verification provisions in any form, make participation voluntary and industry-led, preserve auditor independence from the center, and let the market for assurance mature under the external audit commitments companies have already made. We note that Sections 111 and 112 sunset after three years. Our preference is that they not start at all.

**5. Provisions ACIA supports.**

The draft contains a great deal we support, and we encourage you to keep and fund it: the Section 401 AI testbed program across the Energy Department, NIST and NSF; Section 411's international standards coalitions, which promote private-sector-led standards and counter foreign adversary influence; Section 423's codification of the National AI Research Resource; Section 311's CISA grants for maintainers of critical open-source software (we would remove CAISI's consultation role and let CISA administer the grants); Section 301's reauthorization of the Cybersecurity Act of 2015 through 2035; Section 321's report on model weight, data center and open-source security; Sections 131 and 132's enhanced penalties for AI-enabled fraud and impersonation of federal officials; and Section 122's GAO review, which we would ask to reach permitting bottlenecks as well as energy burdens on AI infrastructure. On Title II, we support Section 243's AI Workforce Research Hub and stand ready to provide technical assistance on Section 251's WARN Act amendments, where the "substantial factor" trigger needs a workable definition. On Section 113, we do not oppose anti-retaliation protections, but recommend that they attach to violations of existing law rather than to the bill's new frontier regime.

**Conclusion.**

The Great American AI Act is the first bipartisan vehicle capable of ending the state patchwork, and we want to help you get it over the line. Our equation is straightforward: permanent preemption, no incident reporting, no codified CAISI, voluntary standards. Deliver that, and America's developers, chipmakers and data center builders will have the one national standard they need to out-innovate the rest of the world. ACIA stands ready to work with you, your staff and the Energy and Commerce Committee ahead of introduction. Please contact Tessa Marchetti, our vice president for policy, to follow up.

Respectfully,

Grant Holloway
President & CEO
American Compute & Innovation Alliance
