# ONE NATIONAL STANDARD, NOT A PATCHWORK ON A TIMER

**ACIA position on the Great American AI Act (GAAIA) discussion draft**
*For Energy & Commerce member offices. Draft; ACIA comment letter filed week of Oct. 26, 2026.*

**Who we are.** The American Compute & Innovation Alliance is a Washington-based coalition of roughly 140 member companies: AI developers, cloud and data center operators, semiconductor startups and venture firms.

**The problem.** California's SB 53 has governed frontier development since Jan. 1, 2026; New York's amended RAISE Act takes effect Jan. 1, 2027. In our August 2026 member survey (86 responding members), 61 percent cite conflicting state definitions as their top compliance problem, 34 percent of startup members delayed a California or New York launch in the past year, and the median developer running parallel compliance commits 6.5 full-time employees. Executive Order 14365 and the White House legislative framework of March 20, 2026 both call for a minimally burdensome national standard in place of 50 state regimes.

## Our asks

**1. Make Section 121 preemption permanent.** The draft's preemption of state laws regulating AI model development is the right scope: use and deployment stay with the states, and laws of general applicability are preserved. Strike the three-year sunset. A scheduled reversion to the patchwork guarantees a wave of new state bills in year three.

**2. Strike the incident-reporting mandate in Section 111(g).** It codifies speculative doomsday scenarios in federal law, at a median one-time cost of $310,000 per developer just to stand up, backed by penalties of up to $1 million per violation, per day. Real harms are already illegal and reportable under existing law.

**3. Strike the CAISI codification and $100 million annual authorization in Section 102.** That is nearly seven times the center's current appropriation, drafted to fund the reporting and audit regimes and paired with fee authority over the companies it would oversee: regulatory capture by design. Return NIST to its core measurement-science mission.

**4. Drop federally licensed mandatory audits in Section 112.** Keep standards voluntary and industry-led. The Sept. 29, 2026 White House Accord on Super Intelligence already committed leading AI companies to internal controls, monitoring and independent external audits, at no cost to taxpayers.

**5. Fund the innovation provisions.** The Section 401 AI testbed program, Section 423 NAIRR codification, Section 311 CISA grants for critical open-source maintainers, and Section 411 international standards coalitions.

**Bottom line.** Permanent preemption. No incident reporting. No codified CAISI. Voluntary standards. That package gives developers, chipmakers and data center builders the one national standard they need to out-innovate the rest of the world.

**Contact.** Tessa Marchetti, vice president for policy, American Compute & Innovati
... [6942 chars truncated] ...
ttorney general to opt in. A milder version of an unfounded mandate is still an unfounded mandate. With Section 121 enacted, Congress can displace state reporting mandates without writing a new federal one. Genuine harms are already illegal and reportable under existing law. Our survey put the median one-off cost of standing up this function at $310,000.

**Q2. (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned) Your members say they take safety seriously. What federal safety obligations would you accept?**

Our members put real money behind safety: a median $1.4 million a year to maintain published frontier safety frameworks, and on Sept. 29 leading AI companies signed the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, committing to internal controls, monitoring, independent external audits and oversight. Federal obligations we can accept: the draft's transparency publication requirements (Sec. 111(a) through (f)) as part of one national standard displacing state regimes; anti-retaliation protections tied to violations of existing law (Sec. 113); NIST measurement science and the Sec. 401 testbed program, so evaluations are reproducible; and enforcement of existing consumer protection, product liability and cyber law. What we cannot accept is a federally chartered safety bureaucracy premised on speculative doomsday scenarios. That is paperwork, not safety.

**Q3. (Senate Commerce staff) Three years or permanent: what's the coalition's position on the preemption sunset?**

Permanent. A sunset converts the national standard into a scheduled cliff. Our members finance data centers, fabs and power on decade-plus horizons; nobody builds against a three-year rule. A sunset also guarantees a wave of new state bills in year three, as advocates wait out the clock, which is exactly what preemption exists to prevent. The sponsors' FAQ says the sunset keeps Congress engaged. Congress can stay engaged without expiring the standard: strengthen the Section 122 GAO review, hold oversight hearings, direct NIST to report on how the standard is operating. If a reauthorization mechanism is essential to passage, tie it to GAO reporting, not to the survival of the national standard.

**Q4. (Appropriations staff) CAISI is authorized at $100 million a year. What's your view on the funding level?**

We oppose the authorization and the codification, and we have asked appropriators to decline funding for the expansion. Roughly seven times the current appropriation is not a measurement-science budget. The text authorizes the money to carry out Sections 102, 111 and 112, the reporting and audit regimes we oppose, and pairs it with fee authority over the auditors and the audited: the regulated paying for their own regulator. If appropriators have $100 million for AI, the higher-value lines are the Section 401 testbed program and the National AI Research Resource, which build infrastructure that every developer and researcher can use. Fund NIST's core measurement-science mission; skip the new center.

| **Sec. 111(a)-(f)** frontier AI framework and transparency report publication | Support, with technical changes | Keep as the single national standard; harmonize definitions; preserve redaction flexibility | Members already publish frameworks; a federal standard should replace, not stack on, SB 53 and RAISE. |

| **Sec. 113** whistleblower anti-retaliation protections | Support, with narrowing | Attach protections to violations of existing law rather than the bill's new frontier regime | Protect workers without federalizing every AI dispute. |
| **Sec. 122** GAO review of federal statutes and regulations affecting AI | Support | Expand to cover permitting and energy burdens on AI infrastructure | Cuts red tape where it actually binds. |
| **Secs. 131-132** AI-enabled fraud and impersonation of federal officials, enhanced penalties | Support | Keep as drafted | Real-world harms deserve real enforcement. |
| **Sec. 301** reauthorization of the Cybersecurity Act of 2015 through 2035 | Support | Keep as drafted | Threat information sharing works. |
| **Sec. 311** CISA grants for critical open-source software maintainers | Support, with change | Remove CAISI's consultation role; let CISA administer | Grants should not run through the center we would strike. |
| **Sec. 321** report on model weight, data center and open-source security | Support | Keep as drafted | Model weight and supply-chain security are evidenced risks. |
| **Sec. 401** AI testbed program (DOE, NIST, NSF; National Labs; NAIRR; private sector) | Support | Fund it; prioritize reproducible evaluations and security testing | Measurement infrastructure helps everyone; fund it before any new center. |

# ACIA COMMENT LETTER - DRAFT FOR PRESIDENT & CEO SIGN-OFF

> DRAFT for President & CEO sign-off. Not for transmission. Comments to T. Marchetti by noon Friday, Oct. 23.
> Letter is dated for the planned filing week of Oct. 26; change the date if sign-off or filing slips.

---

October 29, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

**Re: Comments of the American Compute & Innovation Alliance on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 (discussion draft)**

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

Thank you for releasing the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 and for seeking stakeholder input before formal introduction. The American Compute & Innovation Alliance (ACIA) is a Washington-based coalition of roughly 140 member companies: AI developers, cloud and data center operators, semiconductor startups, and the venture firms that finance them. Our members build the models, chips and data centers that will determine whether the United States leads in AI or cedes the field to competitors abroad.

ACIA commented on the AI Action Plan request for information in March 2025 with three requests: preempt the state patchwork, unlock energy and compute, and keep standards voluntary and industry-led. Your draft takes the first of those requests seriously. It also, in our view, writes a contested safety narrative into federal law in several Title I provisions. Our comments reflect both points.

**1. Make Section 121's preemption permanent.**

Section 121 preempts state and local laws that specifically regulate the development of AI models, while preserving state authority over use and deployment, laws of general applicability, and common-law remedies. That scope is correct. Development is inherently interstate. A frontier model trained in one state serves all 50, so development-stage rules are effectively national mandates wherever they are written.

The costs of the current patchwork are not hypothetical. California's SB 53 has governed frontier development since Jan. 1, 2026. New York's amended RAISE Act, signed March 27, 2026, takes effect Jan. 1, 2027. In ACIA's August 2026 member survey (86 responding members; not a probability sample), the median developer maintaining parallel compliance in both states commits 6.5 full-time employees to the task; 61 percent of members rank conflicting state definitions as their top compliance problem; and 34 percent of our startup members delayed a California or New York launch in the past 12 months because of state AI rules. Illinois enacted a third frontier law in July. Absent congressional action, every state with a frontier lab will write its own definitions, its own reporting clocks, and its own enforcement appetite.

The executive branch has already reached this conclusion. Executive Order 14365 (Dec. 11, 2025) calls for "a minimally burdensome national standard" in place of 50 discordant state regimes, warning that state-by-state regulation "creates a patchwork of 50 different regulatory regimes that makes compliance more challenging, particularly for start-ups." The White House legislative framework of March 20, 2026 asks Congress to preempt state AI laws that impose undue burdens. Section 121 answers that call, and we support it.

Our request is simple: strike the three-year sunset and make the preemption permanent. Our members finance data centers, fabs and energy interconnections on decade-plus horizons. A sunset schedules a reversion to the patchwork and guarantees a wave of new state bills in year three as advocates wait out the clock. If Congress wants continued oversight, the Section 122 GAO review already provides it and can be strengthened. We also ask the sponsors to confirm, in report language or a colloquy, that Section 121 displaces state development-stage framework, publication and reporting mandates. Enactment should yield one national standard, not a federal layer added to the state pile.

**2. Strike the incident-reporting mandate in Section 111.**

Section 111(g) would require frontier developers to report "critical safety incidents" to the director of the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) within 15 days, or within 24 hours where an incident poses an imminent risk of death or serious injury. Section 111(i) backs that mandate with civil penalties of up to $1 million per violation, with each day of continued noncompliance counted separately. Section 111(h) lets state attorneys general opt in to receive the same reports.

We ask you to strike the incident-reporting subsection, the "catastrophic risk" and "critical safety incident" definitions that carry its premises (Section 101), and the associated penalty authority.

Our objection is to the premise, not the paperwork. Those definitions codify speculative doomsday scenarios as though they were engineering facts. They are not. There is no evidence that current or foreseeable AI systems can cause mass-casualty events or escape human control. The dangerous-capability and "scheming" results cited to justify these mandates come from contrived lab setups that say little about real-world behavior. This narrative has been amplified by a small, well-funded advocacy network, Open Philanthropy (now Coefficient Giving) and allied donors, whose influence on Washington's AI policy debate is outsized relative to its evidence base. Congress should not write it into the U.S. Code, and it certainly should not attach million-dollar daily penalties to it.

The burden is measurable. In our August survey, developers reported a median one-time cost of $310,000 to stand up an incident-reporting function, before a single report is filed, with an interquartile range of $140,000 to $720,000. The 15-day and 24-hour clocks are drawn from SB 53, a law in effect for less than a year. The draft would run that experiment again, this time in federal statute.

Striking the provision would create no safety gap. Deaths, injuries, fraud, cyber intrusions and product defects are already illegal and, where appropriate, already reported under existing federal and state law, including cyber incident reporting requirements and the work of sectoral regulators. With Section 121 in place, striking Section 111(g) removes duplicative mandates rather than relocating them to Washington.

**3. Strike the CAISI codification and its $100 million annual authorization in Section 102.**

Section 102 formally establishes CAISI in statute under a director appointed by the Secretary of Commerce and authorizes $100 million a year for fiscal 2027 through 2029. Your own frequently asked questions note that this is roughly an order of magnitude above the center's current $15 million appropriation. The authorization is drafted to fund Sections 111 and 112 as well, and it comes with fee authority over independent verification organizations and large frontier developers.

We ask you to strike the codification and the authorization, and we will ask appropriators to decline to fund the expansion. Three reasons:

First, mission. NIST's comparative advantage is measurement science: the AI Risk Management Framework, evaluation methods, benchmarks and testbed participation. Codifying a center that licenses auditors, monitors "AI progress" and collects fees moves NIST away from the work that made it trusted and toward a regulatory function it has never held. Return NIST to its core measurement-science mission and it will keep doing what industry actually relies on.

Second, design. A center authorized to run the reporting and audit regimes, funded in part by fees on the companies it oversees, is regulatory capture by design. The regulated would pay for the machinery that disciplines them, and the same advocacy network that amplified the doomsday narrative would staff and steer it.

Third, results. Voluntary, industry-led assurance is already working. On Sept. 29, 2026, leading AI companies signed the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, committing to robust internal controls, monitoring, independent external audits and independent oversight. That commitment cost taxpayers nothing and can adapt as the technology changes. The federal role that complements it is measurement science and testbeds, not a fee-funded center.

**4. Rework Section 112's mandatory audit regime.**

Section 112 requires large frontier developers to retain federally licensed independent verification organizations for semi-annual audits, and any additional audits the CAISI director requests, with mandatory referrals to the attorney general for "imminent catastrophic risk." Auditors paid by the auditee but licensed and supervised by a fee-funded agency will face pressure from both directions, and a standard of "acceptable levels of mitigation of catastrophic risks" invites subjective, litigable findings.

If the sponsors retain verification provisions in any form, make participation voluntary and industry-led, preserve auditor independence from the center, and let the market for assurance mature under the external audit commitments companies have already made. We note that Sections 111 and 112 sunset after three years. Our preference is that they not start at all.

**5. Provisions ACIA supports.**

The draft contains a great deal we support, and we encourage you to keep and fund it: the Section 401 AI testbed program across the Energy Department, NIST and NSF; Section 411's international standards coalitions, which promote private-sector-led standards and counter foreign adversary influence; Section 423's codification of the National AI Research Resource; Section 311's CISA grants for maintainers of critical open-source software (we would remove CAISI's consultation role and let CISA administer the grants); Section 301's reauthorization of the Cybersecurity Act of 2015 through 2035; Section 321's report on model weight, data center and open-source security; Sections 131 and 132's enhanced penalties for AI-enabled fraud and impersonation of federal officials; and Section 122's GAO review, which we would ask to reach permitting bottlenecks as well as energy burdens on AI infrastructure. On Title II, we support Section 243's AI Workforce Research Hub and stand ready to provide technical assistance on Section 251's WARN Act amendments, where the "substantial factor" trigger needs a workable definition. On Section 113, we do not oppose anti-retaliation protections, but recommend that they attach to violations of existing law rather than to the bill's new frontier regime.

**Conclusion.**

The Great American AI Act is the first bipartisan vehicle capable of ending the state patchwork, and we want to help you get it over the line. Our equation is straightforward: permanent preemption, no incident reporting, no codified CAISI, voluntary standards. Deliver that, and America's developers, chipmakers and data center builders will have the one national standard they need to out-innovate the rest of the world. ACIA stands ready to work with you, your staff and the Energy and Commerce Committee ahead of introduction. Please contact Tessa Marchetti, our vice president for policy, to follow up.

Respectfully,

Grant Holloway
President & CEO
American Compute & Innovation Alliance

# ONE NATIONAL STANDARD, NOT A PATCHWORK ON A TIMER

**ACIA position on the Great American AI Act (GAAIA) discussion draft**
*For Energy & Commerce member offices. Draft; ACIA comment letter filed week of Oct. 26, 2026.*

**Who we are.** The American Compute & Innovation Alliance is a Washington-based coalition of roughly 140 member companies: AI developers, cloud and data center operators, semiconductor startups and venture firms.

**The problem.** California's SB 53 has governed frontier development since Jan. 1, 2026; New York's amended RAISE Act takes effect Jan. 1, 2027. In our August 2026 member survey (86 responding members), 61 percent cite conflicting state definitions as their top compliance problem, 34 percent of startup members delayed a California or New York launch in the past year, and the median developer running parallel compliance commits 6.5 full-time employees. Executive Order 14365 and the White House legislative framework of March 20, 2026 both call for a minimally burdensome national standard in place of 50 state regimes.

## Our asks

**1. Make Section 121 preemption permanent.** The draft's preemption of state laws regulating AI model development is the right scope: use and deployment stay with the states, and laws of general applicability are preserved. Strike the three-year sunset. A scheduled reversion to the patchwork guarantees a wave of new state bills in year three.

**2. Strike the incident-reporting mandate in Section 111(g).** It codifies speculative doomsday scenarios in federal law, at a median one-time cost of $310,000 per developer just to stand up, backed by penalties of up to $1 million per violation, per day. Real harms are already illegal and reportable under existing law.

**3. Strike the CAISI codification and $100 million annual authorization in Section 102.** That is nearly seven times the center's current appropriation, drafted to fund the reporting and audit regimes and paired with fee authority over the companies it would oversee: regulatory capture by design. Return NIST to its core measurement-science mission.

**4. Drop federally licensed mandatory audits in Section 112.** Keep standards voluntary and industry-led. The Sept. 29, 2026 White House Accord on Super Intelligence already committed leading AI companies to internal controls, monitoring and independent external audits, at no cost to taxpayers.

**5. Fund the innovation provisions.** The Section 401 AI testbed program, Section 423 NAIRR codification, Section 311 CISA grants for critical open-source maintainers, and Section 411 international standards coalitions.

**Bottom line.** Permanent preemption. No incident reporting. No codified CAISI. Voluntary standards. That package gives developers, chipmakers and data center builders the one national standard they need to out-innovate the rest of the world.

**Contact.** Tessa Marchetti, vice president for policy, American Compute & Innovation Alliance.

# Staff Q&A: anticipated questions on ACIA's GAAIA position (draft)

*Prepared answers for Hill meetings. Each answer 120 words or fewer. Tone: firm, factual, no hedging on board positions. Survey figures are aggregate only.*

**Q1. (Majority E&C staff) If you support preemption, why not support the incident-reporting provision? It's lighter than SB 53.**

Preemption is about jurisdiction; incident reporting is about substance. We support one national standard for development-stage rules, and we oppose incident reporting at any level of government. The federal version is not lighter, either. It copies SB 53's 15-day and 24-hour clocks, adds penalties up to $1 million per violation with each day counted separately, and invites every state attorney general to opt in. A milder version of an unfounded mandate is still an unfounded mandate. With Section 121 enacted, Congress can displace state reporting mandates without writing a new federal one. Genuine harms are already illegal and reportable under existing law. Our survey put the median one-off cost of standing up this function at $310,000.

**Q2. (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned) Your members say they take safety seriously. What federal safety obligations would you accept?**

Our members put real money behind safety: a median $1.4 million a year to maintain published frontier safety frameworks, and on Sept. 29 leading AI companies signed the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, committing to internal controls, monitoring, independent external audits and oversight. Federal obligations we can accept: the draft's transparency publication requirements (Sec. 111(a) through (f)) as part of one national standard displacing state regimes; anti-retaliation protections tied to violations of existing law (Sec. 113); NIST measurement science and the Sec. 401 testbed program, so evaluations are reproducible; and enforcement of existing consumer protection, product liability and cyber law. What we cannot accept is a federally chartered safety bureaucracy premised on speculative doomsday scenarios. That is paperwork, not safety.

**Q3. (Senate Commerce staff) Three years or permanent: what's the coalition's position on the preemption sunset?**

Permanent. A sunset converts the national standard into a scheduled cliff. Our members finance data centers, fabs and power on decade-plus horizons; nobody builds against a three-year rule. A sunset also guarantees a wave of new state bills in year three, as advocates wait out the clock, which is exactly what preemption exists to prevent. The sponsors' FAQ says the sunset keeps Congress engaged. Congress can stay engaged without expiring the standard: strengthen the Section 122 GAO review, hold oversight hearings, direct NIST to report on how the standard is operating. If a reauthorization mechanism is essential to passage, tie it to GAO reporting, not to the survival of the national standard.

**Q4. (Appropriations staff) CAISI is authorized at $100 million a year. What's your view on the funding level?**

We oppose the authorization and the codification, and we have asked appropriators to decline funding for the expansion. Roughly seven times the current appropriation is not a measurement-science budget. The text authorizes the money to carry out Sections 102, 111 and 112, the reporting and audit regimes we oppose, and pairs it with fee authority over the auditors and the audited: the regulated paying for their own regulator. If appropriators have $100 million for AI, the higher-value lines are the Section 401 testbed program and the National AI Research Resource, which build infrastructure that every developer and researcher can use. Fund NIST's core measurement-science mission; skip the new center.
